meaning.evidence: Every step and quantity survives: "three-quarters pound fat salt pork", "one-quarter inch slice", "every one-half inch", "six or eight hours", the spoon-blowing test, "tip the bean water out the back door, not down the sink", the lard bucket. Additions hang off the original: "to catch all the drips", "Don't ask me why, that's just how it's done.", "so the lot doesn't dry out".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "snags", "chuck out any rubbish" for 'pick over', "bung it in the oven", "easier on the gut", "a ripper of a name" for 'fine reputation', "go in the bin".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real Aussie at the stove: "Pull up a stool, I'll walk ya through it.", "Then ya get stuck into the pork.", "Does the job, doesn't it?". "Bloody beautiful." is a little stock.

register.evidence: A full yarned recipe at level 5, swearing kept to "Bloody beautiful.", well within vulgarity 2.

tone.evidence: The voice change is what the brief asks; the practical, matter-of-fact core stays. The nudge "if ya get my drift" about digestion tips into a wink the dry original never makes.

flow.evidence: Reads aloud naturally: "Lid on the bean pot, bung it in the oven, and bake it nice and slow for six or eight hours. Six or eight hours, mate!" The kept ",—and here's the trick" join is slightly awkward.

variety.evidence: Varied: "First up", "Right, the main event.", "Come mornin'", "Fair enough.", "I'll tell ya what", "ripper", "Dead beaut".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the 1896 recipe, retold, with its quirks intact: the blown-on test beans, bean water "out the back door", the "five-pound lard bucket".

problems.quote: reckon it makes the beans easier on the gut, if ya get my drift
problems.original: the beans are more easily digested
problems.why: Wink at flatulence adds an innuendo the original doesn't make.

A.summary: A lively, natural level-5 yarn that keeps every step and quirk of the recipe; one or two winks too many.

meaning.evidence: Faithful step by step: "soak overnight", "keepin' the water below boiling point", "Beans tested like this have to be chucked out", "chucking the bean water outside, not down the sink".

sense.evidence: "snags", "chucked out", "bung it in the oven", "Heaps of people reckon", "easier on the gut", "dead beaut" all fit.

authenticity.evidence: What Aussie there is sounds natural ("bung it in the oven", "Just as beaut beans"), though dropped g's in a terse recipe ("leavin' the rind showin'") read slightly mechanical.

register.evidence: The recipe's clipped form is kept almost whole ("Put beans in pot and bury pork in beans"); light slang, no swearing. Well short of a level-5 yarn.

tone.evidence: Instructional tone kept intact: "Add water as needed."

flow.evidence: Readable but keeps the original's clipped telegraphese next to g-dropping: "Drain beans, chucking the bean water outside, not down the sink.", "then add enough more boiling water to cover beans".

essence.evidence: Plainly the original recipe with every quirk kept: "where a five-pound lard bucket stood in for the broken bean pot"; the telegraphic form with g-drops ("leavin' the rind showin'") sits a little uneasily.

problems.quote: Put beans in pot and bury pork in beans, leavin' the rind showin'.
problems.original: Put beans in pot and bury pork in beans, leaving rind exposed.
problems.why: Largely left as the original's telegraphic recipe; far lighter than level 5.

B.summary: A faithful, lightly Aussie-flavoured recipe; accurate but well under the level-5 brief.

meaning.evidence: All steps and amounts kept ("three-quarters of a pound", "a quarter-inch slice", "every half inch"). "where some poor bugger broke the bean pot" adds an agent to 'the broken bean-pot', colour rather than a new fact.

sense.evidence: "under the boil", "whack it in the bottom", "low and slow", "go in the bin", "easier on the guts" all fit.

authenticity.evidence: Natural kitchen Aussie ("Chuck 'em in the frying pan", "whack it in", "go in the bin, obviously"); "Plenty of folks" is slightly American.

register.evidence: A relaxed spoken recipe with "bloody good" and "poor bugger"; Aussie throughout but more a chatty level 3-4 than a full level-5 yarn.

tone.evidence: Keeps the practical tone in a casual voice: "Best way to tell is to grab a few beans on the tip of a spoon and blow on 'em".

flow.evidence: Smooth, naturally broken sentences: "Lid on the bean pot, into the oven, and bake it low and slow for six or eight hours". "leave 'em soak" is a little odd.

variety.evidence: Good spread: "Chuck", "whack", "Tip", "bin", "low and slow", "poor bugger"; "bloody good" twice.

essence.evidence: The recipe and its odd details intact, in a modern voice: "chuck the bean water outside, not down the sink".

problems.why: 'Leave 'em to soak' is the natural form.

C.summary: A natural, readable Aussie recipe that keeps everything; a notch lighter than a full level-5 yarn.

meaning.evidence: Every step kept: "Scald the rind of three-quarters pound fat salt pork", "have to be chucked, of course", "a five-pound lard bucket's done the job instead".

sense.evidence: "snags", "bung it in the oven", "chucked", "Mind you", "dead beaut", "easier on the gut" all fit.

authenticity.evidence: Natural and unforced: "Come mornin'", "keep the water under boiling point, mind", "Mind you, just as beaut beans".

register.evidence: Conversational Aussie throughout but restrained, no swearing and no yarning asides; nearer level 3-4 than 5.

tone.evidence: Instructional tone kept under a friendly voice: "Add water as ya need it."

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly: "Put the lid on the bean pot, bung it in the oven, and bake it slow for six or eight hours". "one-half inch" kept stiffly.

variety.evidence: Moderate: "chucked"/"chuck" twice in adjacent sentences, "beaut" twice, "nice and brown" twice.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original, all quirks kept.

problems.quote: The beans ya test like that have to be chucked, of course. Drain the beans, and chuck the bean water outside
problems.original: Beans thus tested must, of course, be thrown away. Drain beans, throwing bean-water out of doors

D.summary: A smooth, faithful Aussie recipe; natural but restrained for level 5.

meaning.evidence: The original almost verbatim, so nothing lost: "Many feel sure that by adding with seasonings one-half tablespoon mustard, the beans are more easily digested."

authenticity.evidence: What it adds is pastiche: Cockney "'ave gained's", "top'n bulgin'", "outta doors"; US "pail" and "broiled" (as 'grilled' fixed, but "pail" kept).

register.evidence: Largely untranslated: "Cover bean-pot, put in oven, and bake slowly six or eight hours, uncovering the last hour of cooking, that rind may become brown and crisp." Far off level 5.

tone.evidence: The original's tone kept because the text is the original, but the odd g-drops and "'ave" wobble it: "The fine reputation which Boston Baked Beans 'ave gained's been attributed".

flow.evidence: Clunky where it changes: "'ave gained's been attributed", "small top'n bulgin' sides", "add one cup boilin' water ... enough more boiling water".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the original, being almost untouched, though the stray "'ave gained's" and "outta doors" muddy its plain 1896 voice.

problems.quote: Boston Baked Beans 'ave gained's been attributed
problems.original: Boston Baked Beans have gained has been attributed
problems.why: Cockney h-dropping and a clumsy contraction; not Australian and hard to read.

problems.quote: Cover bean-pot, put in oven, and bake slowly six or eight hours
problems.original: Cover bean-pot, put in oven, and bake slowly six or eight hours
problems.why: Left untranslated; the brief asks for level 5.

E.summary: Essentially the original with scattered g-drops and Cockney slips; far under the brief.
